newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CANBERRA WATCH - Work-for-the-dole works for the government.
newsitem.headline: CANBERRA WATCH - Work-for-the-dole works for the government.

text.p: The work-for-the-dole initiative, announced by Prime Minister John Howard on Sunday, is highly effective politics.

Never mind criticisms it creates no jobs, will involve only a small number of young people and provides no meaningful training. Those are details that will have only moderate weight in the minds of voters.
The important message that people will remember will be that phrase "work for the dole", one that many people find instinctively attractive.
Canberra Watch has not been listening to the talkback radio shows today, but there would be no prizes for guessing what the listeners are talking back about.
The Labor opposition criticises this scheme at its peril.
Many commentators have said the government probably timed the announcement to distract attention from the smouldering accusations of expenses fraud.
Work-for-the-dole was probably a little piece of spectacle that the government was preparing for the May budget. The government decided it needed to play the card now.

Note that every minister who had even the remotest thing to say about this initiative (even Health Minister Michael Wooldridge) has participated in an all-singing, all-dancing promotion of the policy today.
In short, the government has pulled out all stops to grab media attention.
Speculating for the moment, Howard must have had a very nasty shock last week when he found his highly prized honesty doubted when he became distantly embroiled in the expenses affair.
Canberra Watch said on Thursday that the expenses matter would probably fade away unless there were further revelations.
There has been another revelation: the police are investigating a second member of the ruling coalition, New South Wales member of parliament Michael Cobb.
Cobb and his colleague Bob Woods, whose expenses claims are also under investigation, have both said they are innocent of wrongdoing.
AND THE LABOUR-FORCE IMPACT?
People who have worked for an hour a week are not counted as unemployed.
So will young people working for their unemployment benefits be counted as employed or unemployed?
The Opposition directly asked Howard for the answer to that question in parliament today.

Howard responded by repeating his earlier assurance that the work-for-the-dole scheme was not "intended" to hide unemployment but said he did not know whether anyone in the government had talked to the Australian Bureau of Statistics about it.
So the question is still open.
